interactions.summary: A student concedes that therapists may have better tools, but argues that the parent still bears the real risk and responsibility for the child.

Jiang translates the therapy dispute into a theological outsourcing test by asking whether God could delegate human guidance to an infinitely wise alien species, and the student defends therapy as noncoercive guidance that preserves free will.

Jiang shuts down the therapy side argument and gives his reading of Dante: Jesus had to die not to satisfy justice or vengeance, but to inspire and educate humanity by rekindling a lost spiritual spark and drawing people back toward God.

claims.claim: A student argues that even if therapists possess specialized tools, the decisive burden still falls on the parent because the parent carries the real risk of what happens to the child.
Jiang tests the logic of delegated redemption by asking whether it would be acceptable for God to skip crucifixion and instead send an infinitely wise alien species to rule and educate humanity.
The therapy-defending student says good therapy works through subtle guidance rather than force and therefore respects human free will instead of overriding it.
Jiang says Dante's explanation of why Jesus had to die is not fundamentally about redemption, justice, or vengeance, but about inspiration and education.
According to Jiang's reading, the sacrifice of Jesus rekindles a lost inner spark, gives people spiritual power, and turns them from being lost in the desert toward the light.
Jiang argues that this reading marks a radical turning point because it shifts Christianity from fear, vengeance, and justice toward love and sacrifice as its operating principle.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes theological outsourcing vivid by asking whether God could have skipped Jesus and governed humanity through an infinitely wise alien species.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest image for why mediated expertise still misses the intimate logic Jiang thinks Dante is trying to explain.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang recasts the crucifixion away from legal payment and toward pedagogy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: It is not about redemption. It's not about justice or vengeance. It's really about inspiration and education
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's core interpretive turn and the hinge for the whole lecture's account of sacrifice.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says Dante's beautiful explanation quietly subverts Catholic theology by replacing fear and vengeance with love and sacrifice.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this beautiful explanation also subverts Catholic theology
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's most consequential claim about how Dante mutates inherited Christian logic from within.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang uses this as the inner capacity rekindled by Jesus's sacrifice, the force that turns lost people back toward God.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet resolves the therapy analogy by turning it into a no-outsourcing model of salvation, then frames Dante's crucifixion logic as a historical shift from fear and vengeance toward love and educational inspiration.
